definition: The study of data whose size, speed, or variety exceeds one computer, using distributed storage and parallel computation.
wrongs: A spreadsheet method that sorts a few thousand rows on a laptop.
A single-server backup that copies one database to a second disk.
A charting step that only changes the colors of an existing report.
why: Big Data Analysis exists because volume, velocity, or variety makes single-machine storage and processing impractical.
example: A city analyzes a year of transit-card taps, too large for one workstation, on a cluster.
scenario: A phone carrier's daily event logs no longer fit or finish on one server. Which subject area studies how to analyze them on a cluster?
scenarioWhy: Data too large or fast for one machine, analyzed with distributed tools, is Big Data Analysis.

definition: The sheer amount of data, large enough that storing or scanning it exceeds one machine.
wrongs: The speed at which new records arrive and must be processed.
The mix of tables, logs, JSON, and media in one collection.
The doubt about whether recorded values are trustworthy.
why: Volume refers to scale in bytes or records, which is why clusters and distributed file systems are used.
example: A science archive holds petabytes of telescope images that cannot fit on one disk.
scenario: A retailer keeps ten years of item-level receipts totaling many terabytes. Which big-data dimension is the main issue?
scenarioWhy: The difficulty is how much data is stored, so the dimension is volume.

definition: The speed at which data are generated and must be ingested or analyzed.
wrongs: The total number of bytes kept in the archive.
The number of different file formats sitting in a lake.
The fraction of fields that fail a quality check.
why: Velocity is about arrival rate and the time available to process each new record.
example: A stock feed delivers millions of quotes per second that a risk screen must see immediately.
scenario: Click events from a game arrive continuously at hundreds of thousands per second. Which dimension dominates the design?
scenarioWhy: The design pressure is how fast events arrive, which is velocity.

definition: The mix of data forms, including tables, logs, JSON, text, images, and other media.
wrongs: The total byte count of one homogeneous table.
The arrival rate of a single sensor stream.
The replication count of one file block.
why: Variety means the collection is not one rigid table, so tools must accept differing structures.
example: A support project joins ticket tables, chat transcripts, and phone-audio files in one analysis.
scenario: An investigation must combine CSV exports, JSON APIs, and PDF scans. Which dimension describes that mix?
scenarioWhy: Several incompatible forms in one analysis are variety.

definition: Uncertainty about data quality, including noise, bias, conflicts, and missing values.
wrongs: The byte size of a data set that forces distributed storage.
The rate at which sensor messages arrive.
The count of file formats stored in a lake.
why: Veracity asks whether values can be trusted, which is separate from how much data there is or how fast it arrives.
example: A health lake contains conflicting patient birth dates from two source hospitals.
scenario: Two source systems disagree on the same customer's address, so analysts doubt the field. Which dimension is that doubt?
scenarioWhy: Distrust caused by conflicting values is a veracity problem.

definition: An open-source framework for storing and processing large data sets across a cluster of ordinary computers.
wrongs: A single-node relational engine limited to memory of one workstation.
A desktop chart tool that only draws bar graphs.
A network switch that routes packets but stores no user files.
why: Hadoop provides distributed storage and job execution so Big Data Analysis can run on many commodity machines.
example: A university cluster runs Hadoop so students can query a multi-terabyte click log.
scenario: A lab wants an open-source cluster stack whose file system and jobs span many cheap servers. Which framework is the usual choice?
scenarioWhy: Hadoop is the open-source framework built to store and process data across ordinary servers.

definition: The distributed file system that splits large files into blocks and stores replicas across a cluster.
wrongs: A resource negotiator that only assigns CPU and memory containers.
An in-memory table API with named columns and a query planner.
A SQL parser that never stores bytes on disk.
why: HDFS is the storage layer: files become large blocks, and copies of those blocks live on data nodes.
example: A 1 terabyte log is cut into large blocks and placed on several servers in the campus cluster.
scenario: Engineers need a file system that breaks a huge log into blocks and keeps copies on different servers. Which component is that?
scenarioWhy: Block storage with replicas across the cluster is HDFS.

definition: A programming model that processes data with a parallel map step and then a key-based reduce step.
wrongs: A file system that only stores block replicas and runs no user function.
A streaming watermark that closes late event windows.
A schema check that rejects rows at load time.
why: Map tasks emit key-value pairs and reduce tasks aggregate all values that share a key.
example: Word-count mappers emit each word with a count of 1, and reducers sum the counts per word.
scenario: A course lab must emit key-value pairs from each input split and then sum values by key. Which model is that?
scenarioWhy: A map over splits followed by a keyed aggregation is MapReduce.

definition: A distributed engine that plans work as a directed graph and can keep intermediate data in memory.
wrongs: A disk block store that only replicates file chunks.
A master that stores only file-namespace metadata.
A batch model that always writes every intermediate result to disk before the next step.
why: Spark builds a job graph and can reuse partitions in memory, which avoids rereading every intermediate result from disk.
example: An iterative page-rank job keeps the current rank vector in memory between Spark stages.
scenario: A machine-learning loop must reuse a multi-gigabyte intermediate data set in memory across passes. Which engine fits that habit?
scenarioWhy: Keeping intermediate partitions in memory between stages is a defining Spark behavior.

definition: Dividing a data set into subsets stored on different nodes so the subsets can be processed in parallel.
wrongs: Copying one entire file onto every node in the cluster.
Enforcing a table schema before any byte is written.
Sorting a final report on a single coordinator only.
why: Each partition can be read and transformed by a local task, which is how parallel jobs divide the work.
example: A sales table is split by country so each country folder is processed by a different worker.
scenario: A daily log is divided by hour into separate pieces, each handled by one worker. Which technique is that division?
scenarioWhy: Splitting the log into independently processed pieces is data partitioning.

definition: Leaving stored files without one enforced schema and applying structure only when a query reads them.
wrongs: Rejecting every row that does not match a declared schema at ingest time.
Requiring a star-schema load before any raw file may land on disk.
Storing only primary-key indexes and no raw payload.
why: The bytes are stored first, and each job interprets columns when it reads, which is the data-lake style.
example: Raw JSON clicks sit in a lake, and a later Spark job projects only the fields that report needs.
scenario: Logs are stored as-is, and two teams apply different column interpretations when they query. Which approach is that?
scenarioWhy: Structure is applied at query time rather than at ingest, which is schema-on-read.

definition: Checking data against a declared schema when it is loaded and rejecting rows that do not fit.
wrongs: Storing raw files first and deciding columns only when a query runs.
Appending events to a log with no column check at all.
Replicating blocks without inspecting their records.
why: The schema is a gate at write time, so later readers can assume the stored table already conforms.
example: A warehouse load rejects a sales row whose date column cannot be parsed as a date.
scenario: A warehouse refuses to insert a row that lacks the declared order-id column. Which policy is that?
scenarioWhy: Validating structure before the row is stored is schema-on-write.

definition: Analysis that uses flexible non-relational stores, such as key-value, document, or wide-column databases, at large scale.
wrongs: A single normalized relational schema enforced on one laptop.
A tape backup format that cannot be queried.
A pixel filter applied to a photograph.
why: These stores scale out and accept evolving or sparse records that are awkward in one rigid relational table.
example: Click documents with differing fields are aggregated in a document database for a product report.
scenario: Event documents have uneven fields and must be aggregated at cluster scale without a fixed relational schema. Which storage style fits?
scenarioWhy: Flexible non-relational storage used for large-scale analysis is NoSQL analytics.

definition: Running a job over a finite data set that is already stored, producing output when the job completes.
wrongs: Updating a result continuously as each new event arrives.
Holding each sample constant between audio sampling instants.
Classifying one image pixel from its neighbors.
why: The input is a bounded, stored collection, and the job runs to completion over that collection.
example: A nightly job recomputes yesterday's complete web-log summaries after the files have landed.
scenario: Each night a job reads the closed sales files for that day and writes a finished summary. Which processing style is that?
scenarioWhy: A completed, stored data set processed as one job is batch processing.

definition: Continuously computing results on events as they arrive, without waiting for a data set to close.
wrongs: Waiting until a full day's files are stored and then starting one job.
Rewriting a whole table only after a manual monthly load.
Sorting one finite CSV on a single machine.
why: The input is unbounded, so operators update results as events flow through the system.
example: A transit dashboard updates passenger counts as each gate scan arrives.
scenario: Fraud scores must update as each card swipe arrives, with no end-of-day file to wait for. Which style is required?
scenarioWhy: Computing on events as they arrive is stream processing.

definition: The HDFS master that stores the directory tree and the map of which DataNodes hold each block.
wrongs: A worker that stores the actual file-block bytes.
A reducer that sums values for one key.
A query planner that optimizes DataFrame operations.
why: Clients ask the NameNode where blocks live, while the file bytes themselves stay on DataNodes.
example: A read of a huge log first asks the NameNode which servers hold the needed blocks.
scenario: A process must look up which servers store the blocks of a path, and it does not hold the file bytes itself. Which role is that?
scenarioWhy: Namespace and block-location metadata, without the block bytes, belong to the NameNode.

definition: A worker that stores HDFS blocks and serves the read and write requests for those blocks.
wrongs: The master that keeps only the file namespace and block map.
A container scheduler that assigns CPU and memory.
A SQL translator that submits jobs but stores no blocks.
why: Block bytes reside on DataNodes, which send those bytes to clients after the NameNode supplies locations.
example: Three servers each keep a copy of one 128 MB block of a lecture-video file.
scenario: A machine on the cluster physically stores file blocks and returns their bytes to readers. Which role is that machine playing?
scenarioWhy: Storing and serving block bytes is the DataNode's job.

definition: Storing multiple copies of each HDFS block on different nodes so the data survive a disk or node failure.
wrongs: Splitting one key across reducers with no extra copies.
Compressing a column so it occupies fewer bytes but has only one copy.
Caching a partition in RAM without writing a durable copy.
why: If one replica is lost, HDFS can still serve the block from another replica.
example: The cluster keeps the usual three copies of each block of a census file on different machines.
scenario: After one disk dies, readers can still open a file because other servers hold the same blocks. Which HDFS feature made that possible?
scenarioWhy: Extra copies of each block on other nodes are block replication.

definition: Hadoop's resource layer that assigns CPU and memory containers on cluster nodes to distributed jobs.
wrongs: The file system that stores replicated data blocks.
A columnar file format used for analytic scans.
A document database that stores JSON records.
why: YARN separates resource scheduling from the storage layer, so different engines can request containers.
example: A Spark job asks YARN for containers on ten workers before its executors start.
scenario: Several engines must share one cluster by requesting CPU and memory containers. Which Hadoop layer grants them?
scenarioWhy: Container scheduling for cluster jobs is YARN.

definition: The MapReduce step that reads an input split and emits intermediate key-value pairs.
wrongs: The step that aggregates all values sharing one key after the shuffle.
The master lookup of block locations.
The final write of a small report to a user's laptop only.
why: Each map task sees one split of the input and independently produces pairs for later grouping.
example: A mapper reads one slice of a novel and emits each word paired with the count 1.
scenario: Each worker reads one input split of a log and outputs pairs of user id and a partial count. Which MapReduce step is that?
scenarioWhy: Reading a split and emitting key-value pairs is the map task.

definition: The MapReduce step that aggregates all values sharing a key after they have been grouped.
wrongs: The step that scans one input split and emits the first key-value pairs.
The copy of a block onto a second DataNode.
The planning of a query that has not started running.
why: After the shuffle groups values by key, the reducer combines those values into a final result per key.
example: One reducer receives every partial count for the word river and outputs the total.
scenario: All partial sums for customer 42 arrive at one worker, which outputs a single total. Which step is that worker performing?
scenarioWhy: Aggregating every value for one key is the reduce task.

definition: The transfer and sort that groups intermediate keys so each reducer receives the values for its keys.
wrongs: The initial split of an input file into map-sized pieces.
The final replication of an output block onto three disks.
The display of a bar chart in a notebook.
why: Pairs must move across the network and be sorted by key before a reducer can see a complete group.
example: Partial word counts travel across the cluster so every count for one word meets at one reducer.
scenario: Map outputs must be moved and grouped by key before reducers can sum them. Which phase does that movement?
scenarioWhy: Network transfer and grouping by key between map and reduce is the shuffle.

definition: An immutable, partitioned Spark collection that remembers its lineage so lost partitions can be recomputed.
wrongs: A mutable spreadsheet cell range stored on one laptop.
The HDFS master metadata file that lists block locations.
A single reducer output file with no record of how it was built.
why: Partitions are immutable and the lineage of transformations lets Spark rebuild a lost partition instead of relying on a copy of every intermediate result.
example: After a worker fails, Spark recomputes one missing partition of a filtered log from the original file.
scenario: A Spark collection is immutable and partitioned, and a lost piece is rebuilt from the record of transformations. What is that collection called?
scenarioWhy: Immutable partitions plus lineage for recomputation define a resilient distributed dataset.

definition: A distributed table of named columns that Spark can optimize with a query planner before running.
wrongs: An untyped bag of opaque blocks with no column names.
A single-row configuration file on the driver only.
A resource manager queue of pending containers.
why: Named columns let the planner push filters and prune columns before the distributed job runs.
example: Analysts select only the fare and distance columns of a distributed taxi table, and Spark skips the other fields.
scenario: A distributed taxi table has named columns, and the engine reorders filters before execution. Which Spark abstraction is that?
scenarioWhy: Named columns plus planner optimization describe a Spark DataFrame.

definition: Delaying Spark work until an action needs a result, so transformations can be planned together.
wrongs: Running every transformation immediately as soon as the line of code is called.
Writing each intermediate RDD fully to HDFS before the next call returns.
Starting reducers before any map task has been scheduled.
why: Transformations only build a plan, and an action such as a count or a write triggers execution of that plan.
example: Two filter calls on a log build a plan, and nothing is read until a count action runs.
scenario: A student chains filters and a select, and the cluster stays idle until a write action is called. Which Spark behavior is that?
scenarioWrongs: A forced disk write after each step
scenarioWhy: Waiting for an action before running the planned transformations is lazy evaluation.

definition: A Spark step in which each output partition depends on a single input partition, so no shuffle is required.
wrongs: A step that must regroup keys from many partitions across the network.
A full sort of every record by one key across the cluster.
A join that matches a large table to another large table on a key.
why: Because each parent partition feeds at most one child partition, the work stays local and no exchange is needed.
example: A map that converts each taxi row's fare from cents to dollars touches each partition independently.
scenario: A per-row fare conversion never moves records between workers. Which kind of Spark transformation is that?
scenarioWhy: A per-partition map with no data exchange is a narrow transformation.

definition: A Spark step in which an output partition depends on many input partitions, requiring a shuffle.
wrongs: A filter that keeps or drops each record inside its current partition.
A type cast applied independently on every partition.
Reading a file split that already sits on the local disk.
why: Records with the same key must be brought together from many partitions, which is a shuffle.
example: Grouping taxi trips by driver id moves rows so each driver's trips meet in one partition.
scenario: Grouping trips by driver id forces records to move across the cluster. Which kind of transformation is that?
scenarioWhy: A group-by that reshuffles keys across partitions is a wide transformation.

definition: An imbalance in which one partition holds far more data than the others and delays the whole stage.
wrongs: A perfectly even split of keys across every reducer.
A higher replication factor on every block.
A faster network that shortens every shuffle equally.
why: The stage cannot finish until the overloaded partition finishes, so one hot key stalls the job.
example: One celebrity account owns most of the clicks, so its reducer runs for hours while other reducers finish quickly.
scenario: One key owns 90 percent of the events, and its task runs long after the other tasks finish. Which problem is that?
scenarioWhy: One oversized partition holding up the stage is partition skew.

definition: Increasing capacity by adding more machines rather than by replacing one machine with a larger one.
wrongs: Adding CPUs and disks only inside the same single server.
Compressing a file so one laptop can open it.
Deleting old partitions until the data fit in memory.
why: Big Data Analysis grows a cluster outward, distributing partitions across the added nodes.
example: When a nightly job starts missing its deadline, the team adds four more servers to the cluster.
scenario: A pipeline is slow, and the team adds nodes instead of buying a bigger single computer. Which scaling approach is that?
scenarioWhy: Adding machines to share the work is horizontal scaling.

definition: Inexpensive ordinary servers used together in a cluster instead of one specialized high-end computer.
wrongs: A custom mainframe that is the only machine allowed to store the data.
A laptop used as the permanent production store.
A tape robot that cannot run computation.
why: Hadoop-style systems expect many cheap servers, with software handling failures instead of exotic hardware.
example: A startup builds its lake on racks of standard two-socket servers from a catalog.
scenario: A design brief says to use many ordinary servers and let software tolerate failures. Which hardware approach is that?
scenarioWhy: Clusters of ordinary servers are commodity hardware.

definition: Continuing a job after a node fails by reading a replica or recomputing lost partitions.
wrongs: Stopping the entire cluster permanently when any one disk reports an error.
Ignoring input checksums and writing partial answers as if they were complete.
Requiring a human to retype lost records before the job may resume.
why: Replicas and lineage let the system replace lost pieces without restarting the whole analysis from scratch by hand.
example: When one worker dies mid-job, Spark recomputes that worker's partition and the query still returns.
scenario: A DataNode crashes during a query, yet the job finishes by using other copies and recomputation. Which property is being shown?
scenarioWhy: Finishing after a node loss by replica reads or recomputation is fault tolerance.

definition: Scheduling a task on a node that already stores the block it needs, to avoid a network read.
wrongs: Always shipping every block to one fixed coordinator before computation.
Randomly placing tasks with no regard to where blocks live.
Storing the namespace on the same disk as every user block.
why: Moving the program to the data is cheaper than moving large blocks across the network.
example: Hadoop starts a map task on the server that already holds the log block being counted.
scenario: The scheduler prefers to run a task on the server that already has the needed block. Which principle is that?
scenarioWrongs: Always reading at a central node
Putting metadata on every block disk
scenarioWhy: Placing the task where the block already resides is data locality.

definition: An optional local aggregation of map output on the same node, used to shrink data before the shuffle.
wrongs: The final authority that replaces the reducer and runs on a different set of keys.
A NameNode checkpoint of the namespace.
A schema file stored beside a columnar data file.
why: The combiner partially aggregates pairs locally so fewer bytes cross the network, without changing a compatible final reduce.
example: Each mapper sums its own word counts before sending much smaller totals into the shuffle.
scenario: Word-count mappers add local counts before the network transfer so less data moves. Which optional step is that?
scenarioWrongs: A replacement reducer on other keys
scenarioWhy: Local pre-aggregation of map output before the shuffle is a combiner.

definition: Starting a duplicate copy of a slow task and keeping whichever copy finishes first.
wrongs: Deleting a slow task and marking its input as empty.
Moving the NameNode onto the slowest worker.
Disabling replication while a job is late.
why: A straggler may be stuck on a unhealthy node, so a second attempt elsewhere can finish the task sooner.
example: One map task stalls, Hadoop launches a second copy on another node, and the first copy to finish is kept.
scenario: A straggler task is duplicated on another node, and the faster copy's result is kept. Which Hadoop behavior is that?
scenarioWhy: Launching a backup attempt of a slow task is speculative execution.

definition: A SQL-like warehouse layer that queries data in HDFS and translates statements into distributed jobs.
wrongs: A block-storage daemon that only serves file chunks.
A container scheduler with no query language.
A stream watermark used to close event-time windows.
why: Hive exposes tables and a SQL-like language while the execution still runs as cluster jobs on the stored files.
example: An analyst writes a SQL-like query over a year of logs in HDFS, and Hive launches the underlying jobs.
scenario: Business students query HDFS tables with SQL-like statements that compile into cluster jobs. Which layer are they using?
scenarioWhy: SQL-like queries translated into jobs over HDFS data are Hive.

definition: Laying out values of each column together so a query can read only the columns it needs.
wrongs: Storing each entire record contiguously so every query reads every field.
Storing only keys and discarding values.
Keeping one row per file with no column grouping.
why: Analytic scans often touch a few columns of many rows, and contiguous columns make that scan cheaper.
example: A fare analysis reads only the price column of a huge trip table and skips rider names.
scenario: A report needs 2 columns from a 200-column table and should not read the other fields. Which layout helps most?
scenarioWhy: Grouping values by column lets the scan skip unneeded fields.

definition: A compressed columnar file format widely used for analytical tables in Hadoop and Spark.
wrongs: A row-oriented exchange format whose schema travels with the records.
A resource-manager protocol for requesting containers.
A stream processor that only handles event time.
why: Parquet stores columns contiguously with compression and statistics, which suits selective analytic reads.
example: A Spark job writes taxi trips as Parquet so later fare queries skip unused columns.
scenario: A team stores a warehouse table in a compressed columnar format for Spark scans. Which format is the common choice?
scenarioWhy: The common compressed columnar analytic format on this stack is Parquet.

definition: A row-oriented binary format that stores records together with a schema, often for data exchange.
wrongs: A columnar scan format designed so queries skip unread fields.
An in-memory Spark table API.
A block-replication policy inside HDFS.
why: Avro writes records row by row and keeps a schema so producers and consumers agree on fields.
example: An ingest service writes click events as Avro messages that a later job deserializes with the same schema.
scenario: Services exchange complete records in a compact binary form that carries a schema, row by row. Which format fits?
scenarioWhy: Row-oriented binary records with a schema are Avro.

definition: A NoSQL model that stores each record as a unique key and an opaque value for fast lookups.
wrongs: A model of self-describing documents with many named fields.
A model of sparse column families inside each row key.
A relational model that requires joins across normalized tables.
why: The access path is the key, and the value can be retrieved without a relational join.
example: A session store fetches a user's cart by session id and returns one opaque blob.
scenario: An application retrieves each shopping cart by a single id and does not query inside the payload. Which NoSQL model matches?
scenarioWhy: Lookup by a unique key of an opaque value is the key-value model.

definition: A NoSQL model that stores self-describing records, often JSON-like, so fields can differ across records.
wrongs: A model that allows only one opaque blob per key and no field names.
A model that stores fixed relational rows with a schema enforced on write.
A model used only to place HDFS block replicas.
why: Each document carries its own fields, which lets analysts store evolving event structures.
example: Product reviews are stored as JSON documents, some with photos and some without.
scenario: Events are JSON objects whose fields differ by event type and must stay queryable. Which NoSQL model fits?
scenarioWhy: Self-describing JSON-like records with varying fields are the document model.

definition: A NoSQL model that stores rows with large numbers of sparse, grouped columns for big analytical tables.
wrongs: A model of one opaque value per key with no columns.
A three-column relational table that forbids extra fields.
A pixel grid used for image filtering.
why: Column families can be sparse and very wide, which suits tall analytical data such as time series per row key.
example: A metrics store keeps one row per device and a huge sparse set of timestamped measurement columns.
scenario: Each device row needs a huge sparse set of timestamp columns, not one opaque blob. Which NoSQL model fits?
scenarioWhy: Rows with many sparse grouped columns are the wide-column model.

definition: The claim that during a network partition a distributed store cannot guarantee both strong consistency and full availability.
wrongs: The claim that every store can be consistent, available, and partition-tolerant at the same time.
A rule that replication factor must equal the number of columns.
A statement that batch jobs are always faster than streaming jobs.
why: When messages between nodes fail, the system must either refuse some requests or serve data that may not be the latest.
example: During a split between data centers, a cart service either rejects writes or accepts writes that replicas have not all seen.
scenario: A partition separates two data centers, and designers must choose between up-to-date reads and answering every request. Which theorem frames that choice?
scenarioWrongs: A claim that all three goals hold together
scenarioWhy: The consistency-versus-availability choice during a partition is the CAP theorem.

definition: A guarantee that replicas will agree if new updates stop, even if reads briefly disagree.
wrongs: A guarantee that every read sees the latest write immediately on all nodes.
A guarantee that a partition never happens.
A guarantee that schemas are checked before every write.
why: Updates propagate asynchronously, so replicas converge once the system is given time without new conflicting writes.
example: A profile edit shows on one server immediately and on a second server a few seconds later.
scenario: Two replicas of a shopping cart may differ for a short time, but they match after updates pause. Which guarantee is that?
scenarioWhy: Temporary disagreement that disappears after updates stop is eventual consistency.

definition: A design with a batch layer for accurate recomputation, a speed layer for recent data, and a serving layer that merges them.
wrongs: A stream-only design that reprocesses history from one log and has no separate batch layer.
A single nightly batch with no path for recent events.
A cache of one laptop file with no serving tier.
why: The batch layer recomputes correct views, while the speed layer covers data the batch has not absorbed yet.
example: A dashboard reads a nightly master count and adds a fast layer of clicks that arrived since midnight.
scenario: A product keeps an accurate batch view and a separate fast view of the latest hour, merged for queries. Which architecture is that?
scenarioWhy: A batch layer plus a speed layer merged at query time is the lambda architecture.

definition: A stream-only design that serves both live results and reprocessed history from one log, without a separate batch layer.
wrongs: A design that always pairs a batch layer with a distinct speed layer.
A warehouse that only runs a monthly cube build.
A file system that only replicates blocks.
why: Reprocessing means replaying the same log through the stream pipeline, so a second batch codebase is unnecessary.
example: To fix a bug, engineers replay the click log through the same streaming job that handles live clicks.
scenario: A team handles both live traffic and historical corrections by replaying one log, with no second batch system. Which architecture is that?
scenarioWhy: One stream pipeline for live data and replayed history is the kappa architecture.

definition: A grouping of events by the time they occurred, not by the time the system received them.
wrongs: A grouping based only on when the server happened to process each event.
A grouping of rows by a customer id with no time involved.
A fixed HDFS block size used for every file.
why: Event time stays meaningful even when events arrive late or out of order.
example: Gate scans are counted by the minute printed on the scan, even if a phone uploads the scan late.
scenario: Late-arriving ticket scans must still count in the minute they were scanned, not the minute they were uploaded. Which window basis is that?
scenarioWhy: Bucketing by when the event happened is an event-time window.

definition: A moving event-time threshold that states how late an event can be and still enter its window.
wrongs: A disk usage alert that only measures how full HDFS is.
A schema version number stored in a table catalog.
A replication factor printed in a file report.
why: The watermark estimates progress in event time so the engine can close windows while still allowing limited lateness.
example: A job treats scan time as complete up to 2 minutes ago and drops scans older than that watermark.
scenario: A streaming count closes a minute once event time is judged to have passed it by 2 minutes. Which marker tracks that lateness bound?
scenarioWhy: The lateness bound that lets windows close is a watermark.

definition: Processing a stream as a sequence of small batches collected over short time intervals.
wrongs: Processing one unbounded event at a time with no batch boundary at all.
Waiting for a full closed day before any computation starts.
Storing a file once and never computing on new arrivals.
why: Each short interval becomes a tiny batch job, which is how classic Spark Streaming handles streams.
example: A dashboard recomputes click totals every two seconds from the events collected in that slice.
scenario: A Spark stream job runs a small batch every few seconds instead of one record at a time or one nightly job. Which style is that?
scenarioWhy: Repeated short batches over a stream are micro-batch processing.

definition: A large store of raw data kept in its original formats until a specific analysis needs it.
wrongs: A tightly modeled warehouse that accepts only cleaned rows matching a star schema.
A single CSV on a laptop desktop.
A cache of query results with the raw sources deleted.
why: The lake retains raw variety at scale so different jobs can apply schema-on-read later.
example: An airline keeps raw JSON bookings, CSV delays, and text complaints together in one lake.
scenario: A company stores raw logs, dumps, and media in place and interprets them only when jobs run. Which repository style is that?
scenarioWrongs: A result cache with sources deleted
scenarioWhy: Keeping raw data in native formats for later interpretation is a data lake.

definition: Loading raw data into the cluster first and transforming it there, instead of transforming everything before the load.
wrongs: Cleaning and reshaping every record on a separate server before any byte reaches the cluster.
Deleting raw data and keeping only a final chart image.
Replicating blocks with no transformation step at any time.
why: The cluster has the scale to transform data after landing, which matches schema-on-read lakes.
example: Click files land raw in the lake overnight, and a morning Spark job builds the cleaned session table.
scenario: Raw files are loaded first, and the heavy cleanup runs inside the cluster afterward. Which pipeline pattern is that?
scenarioWhy: Load first and transform inside the platform is ELT.
